Where these fail, the service sectors are interpolated between 1940 and the first post-war observation, and the movement between 1943 and 1945 is taken from the Lithuanian ratios. The estimates for 1941--5 are therefore `rough' in Feinstein's sense, with a margin of 15--25 per cent, and the 1944 trough is an order of magnitude rather than a measurement \parencite[21]{feinstein1972}. Because the Soviet-period series is extrapolated backwards through the war, an error in the wartime linkage would shift its level in 1937--40, so that the overlap tests the linkage together with the rest of the extrapolation; the spliced series, which follows the interwar series to 1940, is affected only through the 1940 average. \subsection{Population and borders} Latvia's borders changed once, when the eastern Abrene district was transferred to the Russian republic in 1944. The series to 1944 refer to the borders of the republic and the series from 1945 to present-day borders. This is the convention of the Maddison Project, which treats income per head as unaffected by a territorial change that moves less than a third of the population \parencites[629]{maddison_project_paper2014}[30]{bolt_zanden_newgdp2021}; the transferred district held a few per cent of the pre-war population at most \parencites[74]{years_of_dependence}[129--30]{hiden_salmon}, and was rural and poorer than the national average, so that the break in income per head is small and no adjustment has been made. The population series rests on the censuses of 1920, 1925, 1930, 1935, 1959, 1970, 1979 and 1989 and the year-end estimates of the Latvian statistical office and the `Baltic 100' database, with mid-year figures as the average of consecutive year-ends; wartime losses, the flight of some 120,000 ethnic Latvians to the West in 1944 \parencite[86]{king_1965_economic}, the Holocaust and the deportations are taken from the demographic literature, and the Soviet garrison of 1940--1 is added to the resident population.
